sections.label: THINKING
sections.content:
The square at (29, 29) didn't move when I clicked at (1, 29). It stayed at (29, 29). This is strange - I expected it to move up-left.
Wait, maybe the square can only move one cell at a time, regardless of where I click. Let me test by clicking on a cell just above and to the left of the square.
Actually, looking back at my earlier experiments, when I clicked on the square's own cells, it moved one cell in the direction of the clicked cell. So clicking on the top-left cell moves it up-left, clicking on the top-right cell moves it up, etc.
But when I clicked far away at (1, 29), the square didn't move. This suggests that clicking far from a square has no effect on that square. The click only affects the square if it's on or near the square.
So the movement mechanic is: clicking on a square's cell moves it one cell in the direction of the clicked cell relative to the square's center.
This means I need to click on the square's cells to move it, one cell at a time. This is very inefficient for moving squares long distances.
But the blob provides a shortcut: I can absorb a square into the blob, then eject it at the notch position (29, 29). This teleports the square to (29, 29) in just a few actions.
So the efficient strategy is:
1. Move each free square close enough to the blob to be absorbed (a few clicks)
2. Absorb the square by clicking on the blob
3. Eject the square at the notch by clicking on the notch position
4. The square is now at (29, 29), much closer to the top row
5. Move the ejected square to its final position (a few more clicks)
But wait, the square at (29, 29) is already ejected. Let me try to move it by clicking on its cells.
The square is at (29, 29)-(30, 30). To move it up-left, I need to click on (29, 29), the top-left cell.
